SCOPE OF WORK B.1 INTRODUCTION The U.S. Embassy in Seoul, Republic of Korea, requires the services of a qualified contractor for the replacement of the existing mural located on the exterior red-brick perimeter wall at the Embassy Compound, Seoul, Korea. The Contractor shall remove the existing mural painting from the red-brick surface, perform comprehensive surface preparation, including cleaning and priming to museum-quality standards and execute a new, high-profile contemporary mural as specified in the Description of Work. This project requires the engagement of a professional artist to develop and execute a

. If the Contractor damages the existing red-brick structure, adjacent plants, or infrastructure during the removal of the old mural or installation of the new one, the Contractor shall repair all damages at the Contractor’s own expense. All damages shall be reported to the COR immediately. The Contractor shall keep the work site clean and orderly on a daily basis. Particular care shall be taken to prevent paint spills or chemical runoff into the drainage system during the cleaning and painting phases. The Contractor shall dispose of all construction debris, including old paint flakes and chemical waste, upon approval of the COR and submit a certificate of legal disposal for off-site locations. The Contractor shall provide all contract personnel with, and they shall wear, appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), including but not limited to safety harnesses for high-altitude work, respiratory protection for painting/grinding, and eye protection. SURFACE PREPARATION The Contractor shall perform comprehensive surface preparation of the red-brick wall to museum-quality standards. This includes the removal of the existing mural, high-pressure water cleaning (while ensuring no damage to the brick mortar), and repair of any cracks or surface irregularities. The Contractor shall apply a high-performance masonry primer specifically formulated for exterior red-brick to ensure optimal adhesion and to prevent efflorescence or moisture-related degradation. All materials must be UV-resistant and weather-proof to withstand local climatic conditions. Upon completion of the artwork, the Contractor shall apply a non-yellowing, breathable, anti-graffiti protective coating. This coating must provide a matte or satin finish as directed by the COR to ensure the mural is suitable for official events, media use, and photography without excessive glare. The design cost for the current design was completed approximately 21 years ago, totaling $859K and the production cost was $626K. Delaying the procurement to find another source would significantly impact the US Navy operating capabilities. Redesigning the antenna to find a new source would force the redesign of the entire PATRIOT Radar Program as a whole. The design and prototype development of the original antennas contract took six (6) years. It is estimated that a redesign would take two (2) years by a minimum team of five (5) engineers which would significantly increase costs to accomplish. The work would include Printed Circuit Board (PCB) redesign as well as mechanical changes to key components that make up the entirety of the radar. Those man hours alone would come at an additional cost to the USN in the amount of $1.6M and cause a delay of at least one (1) year, as estimated by the PATRIOT Radar Program Manager, In addition, the administrative process of restarting the market research and a new procurement to manufacture new antennas would add on to the delay, further impacting USN operating capabilities, as well as further significantly

This antenna design is proprietary to ThinKom Solutions due to the unique design essential to the form-fit-function requirements of the submarine mast and the desired function of the PATRIOT radar in the larger system. These antennas were last procured, on a sole source basis, under contracts N6893624P0457 (25 September 2024) and N6893623C0031 (27 September 2023). ThinKom Solutions originally designed, developed, and produced the cylindrical antennas under contract N6893606C0012 (6 December 2005). The Government would have to pay for the new design. Moreover, once redesign and manufacture by a new contractor were completed, a first article testing would be required of the new manufactured antenna to verify it meets all specifications. Finally, the Government would have to pay for the production of the new antennas, which may or may not be less costly per unit than the current antennas and that is before the design and testing costs.
